To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
spider phobia is characterized by increased vigilance and preferential responding to phobia-relevan stimuli.
spider phobics showed increased early posterior negativity and late positive potential during the encoding of spider pictures compared to non-phobic controls.
spider phobia participants respond with larger P1 and EPN amplitudes to spider pictures compared to non-fearful controls.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how emotional information is processed by the brain.
the study of brain dynamics of spider phobic individuals exposed to emotional stimuli.
the question of the temporal unfolding of perceptual and emotional processing in spider-phobic and nonfearfull controls.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the P1 effect in spider phobia is not fear-specific but rather reflects an increased attention to emotional stimuli in general.
the P1 effect reflects an unspecific vigilance effect whereas the EPN and the LPP are specific to phobia-related stimuli.
the observed effects of increased attentional allocation and emotional responding in spider phobia individuals are not specific to phobic stimuli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the P1 component is related to unspecific vigilance to the emotional content of the stimuli, the EPN and LTP are related to preferential responding to phobia-relevent stimuli.

spider phobia individuals show a more general increase in attentional processing of all emotional stimuli, whereas at later processing stages, phobia-relevant stimuli seem to be preferentially processed.
spider phobia is a disorder of perceptual attention, which is not specific for the phobia-relevant stimulus but rather a general feature of emotional processing in spider phobics.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the brain dynamics underlying phobic fear can be studied in a highly ecologically valid way by using dense sensor event-related brain potential (ERPs) measures in conjunction with emotional picture stimuli.
the P1 effect is not a fear specific response, but rather a general response to any emotional stimulus.
the EPN and LPS may be useful for identifying the emotional relevance of a stimulus and may be a promising tool to investigate emotional processing in phobia.
